extracted.intended_audience: researchers and developers in computational humor, NLP and automated joke-generation systems
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating a computational framework (GOOFER) that learns to generate short jokes from human-rated example jokes by extracting templates/schemas, computing humor metrics, and using machine learning (classification/regression) as an aggregator.

rubrics_metrics.name: OBVIOUSNESS
rubrics_metrics.description: The first (obvious) interpretation of the setup should be very obvious; otherwise observers will not experience an incongruity when the hidden interpretation is forced by the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximate with association or semantic distance in a lexicon (closer words imply more obvious interpretation) and unigram frequency (high frequency indicates common/obvious meanings). Example: words not far semantically likely link to the same common interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: CONFLICT
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a conflict between the punchline and the obvious interpretation, sufficient to start the cognitive search process for a hidden interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximate using association or semantic distance (larger distances correlate with higher conflict). N-gram co-occurrence statistics can help detect when punchline words emphasize a different meaning than the obvious interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: COMPATIBILITY
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of the punchline should be compatible with the hidden interpretation so the search stops on a single cognitive rule rather than resulting in puzzlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximate with n-gram frequencies (higher co-occurrence indicates compatibility), word ambiguity measures (number of senses), and phonetic/homophone similarity where homonyms link the two interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: COMPARISON
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a contrasting/contrasting relationship between the two possible interpretations of the setup (bisociation); without contrast there is no bisociation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure contrast by analyzing domains (e.g., WordNet Domains) or semantic distance; adjective vector differences and differences in adjective distributions for nouns have been used to approximate contextual contrast between interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: INAPPROPRIATENESS
rubrics_metrics.description: The second interpretation should be odd, inappropriate, taboo or otherwise unexpected, which makes it less obvious and more humorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximate via unigram frequency in a balanced corpus (low frequency -> unpredictable), 'sexiness' metrics comparing frequency in sexual vs non-sexual corpora, and other corpus-based measures of oddness/absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric set must cover the five IR properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The chosen set of computational metrics/features should cover OBVIOUSNESS, CONFLICT, COMPATIBILITY, COMPARISON and INAPPROPRIATENESS to form a theoretically-founded knowledge base for humor judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select at least one metric representing each IR property; the knowledge base is extensible and metrics can complement each other. Validate metrics by mapping them to the five properties and ensure coverage rather than exhaustiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical schema — Header
rubrics_metrics.description: A schema must include a header: the name of the schema and the variables used in the schema.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Header binds the schema components and is transferable from constraint-based schemas; should identify which template slots will be scored by which metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical schema — Generator
rubrics_metrics.description: A metrical schema must define a generator component that proposes candidate template values for jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The generator can be any method (n-grams, another template-based system, neural generator). It should accept seeds and per-variable constraints (e.g., POS) to reduce the search space and increase classifier-assigned scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical schema — Features
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the features (metrics) used and which template variables they apply to; features map template values to numeric values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features can be corpus frequencies, semantic distances, ambiguity counts, vector similarities, sexual-frequency ratios, etc. Apply features to all valid combinations of template values that meet prerequisites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical schema — Aggregator
rubrics_metrics.description: Define an aggregator that combines feature values to choose output jokes (e.g., thresholding, sum/comparison, or a learned classifier/regressor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregators can be rule-based, minimization products (as prior work), or learned models (classification/regression). For learned aggregators, choose thresholds for 'good' output and account for noise and metric sparsity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical schema — Template
rubrics_metrics.description: A template is the textual skeleton with slots for variables into which chosen template values are inserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Templates in this paper are fixed strings with slots; future work recommends grammars for flexible grammatical variations (grammar trees allowing minimal generalizations like same word, same stem, same POS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical schema — Keywords
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the most relevant variables (keywords) used to calculate equivalence between schema outcomes and avoid producing overly similar jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keywords are used to detect and filter near-duplicates to maintain surprise and avoid boring repetition for users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schema generalization requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent existing constraint-based and other generators as metrical schemas so the framework can incorporate diverse generator types and enable machine learning-based aggregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map constraint checks to features (0/1), map multiple templates via concatenation, and define a generator that enumerates combinations if needed for theoretical mapping — enabling a strictly more general notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification vs Regression schema choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose classification algorithms to predict discrete ratings (mode or individual scorer) and regression algorithms to predict continuous scores (average rating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regression can use average ratings but may blur individual differences; classification uses discrete classes. Select based on the rating aggregation strategy and training data characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifier/regressor properties: noise resistance and interpretability
rubrics_metrics.description: The chosen ML aggregator should be robust to noisy features and, where useful, interpretable so humans can learn which metrics matter for a template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random Forests are recommended for noise resistance; decision trees (or tree-based models) provide attribute importance or readable rules. Consider trade-offs between robustness and explainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human evaluation / rated examples requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Human-rated example jokes are required for training the classifier/regressor to distinguish good from bad jokes; humans provide the only supervised signal in GOOFER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect ratings (possible aggregation via mode or average). Ensure enough labeled examples per template. The paper used crowdsourced ratings and reports example evaluation statistics (e.g., percent >=4 stars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Template extractor functionality and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Template extractor must detect templates from example jokes, extract template values (and metadata like POS), and cluster similar templates to increase data per template.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing template extractors (T-PEG) detect variable types and hidden variables; clustering can merge templates (examples: T-PEG 69.2% usable templates, another system 61% precision). Future work: extract grammars rather than fixed strings and define distance measures for grammar trees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric-based rater behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric-based rater must compute the identified metrics for each candidate template value (or combinations) and map template values to numeric feature vectors for ML.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply every applicable metric on all combinations of template values that fit prerequisites. Be aware this produces many (potentially noisy) features — choose algorithms that handle high-dimensional noisy input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Values generator constraints and design
rubrics_metrics.description: The values generator should propose candidate template values suited to the template (e.g., respecting part-of-speech constraints), using any generation technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using POS and template metadata reduces generative space and improves average classifier scores. N-gram based generators are simple and effective for single-word slots; existing humor systems can be reused as generators inside GOOFER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keywords/equivalence filtering to preserve surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Use keywords and equivalence measures to avoid outputting highly similar jokes that would reduce surprise for the user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute equivalence on specified keyword variables and filter near-duplicates; this maintains novelty and surprise which are essential for humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregator acceptance thresholding
rubrics_metrics.description: Define thresholds (score cutoffs) on classifier/regressor outputs to decide which generated template value combinations are considered 'good' enough to output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thresholds can be absolute or relative; for classification use class labels, for regression pick minimum predicted score. Threshold selection affects precision/recall of humorous outputs and should be tuned on validation data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training dataset design and simplifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Training data design choices (e.g., restricting to a single template, single-word template values) simplify template extraction and generation but constrain generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplifications speed up data collection and mapping but future systems should relax these (support multi-word values, multiple templates, grammatical variants) to increase coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics for generated jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate generation effectiveness with user ratings and comparative baselines (e.g., percent generated jokes achieving >=4/5 stars vs human-created baseline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare generated output quality to human-produced jokes under similar constraints. Example result: GAG achieved 11.41% jokes ≥4 stars vs human 21.08% for similar constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensibility and knowledge-base updating
rubrics_metrics.description: The metrics knowledge base should be extensible to add new metrics for specific joke types or to test new humor theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow adding new features and re-training per template; this supports adapting to temporal and individual preferences by feeding back rated generated jokes into the training data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of probabilistic logic for human-comprehensible schemas
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider probabilistic logic (e.g., ProbLog) to obtain probabilistic schemas that combine metrical features with more human-readable probabilistic rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probabilistic logic could upgrade constraint-based schemas to a probabilistic paradigm, facilitating human comprehension and co-creation of specifications between humans and machines.
